## Why do we need an extra week on this?

Base ```R``` is limited for data manipulation and visualization

It can be:

- Hard to read, especially across languages
- Inefficient (many lines of code to perform a common operation)

## What is Base ```R```

"Base ```R```" $=$ What is available in ```R``` with no added packages.

Note: There are benefits to Base ```R```.

- "Lightweight" (no additional time/space to install)
- Especially stable across updates

## What is the alternative?

"Tidyverse" describes a suite of ```R``` packages supported by Posit

Information at: [https://tidyverse.org](https://tidyverse.org)

Associated with "R for Data Science": [https://r4ds.hadley.nz](https://r4ds.hadley.nz)

Install it!

## What will we learn about the "Tidyverse"?

We will learn about:

- ```dplyr```: Helps filter and aggregate data
- ```ggplot2```: Helps create nice plots

## Getting Ready to Explore ```dplyr```

We're going to use ```dplyr``` to summarize data on flights that departed New York City from JFK, LGA, or EWR in 2013.

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
library(nycflights13)  
library(dplyr)
flights <- nycflights13::flights
```

## The Flights Data is a ```tibble```

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
str(flights)
```

## Converting the Flights Data to a Data Frame

To avoid learning about a new data structure, we'll convert the ```tibble``` to a data frame.

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
flights <- as.data.frame(flights)
```

## The ```filter``` Function

Allows us to easily subset data according to the values that a variable takes on

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
filter(flights, month == 1, day == 1)
```

Previously we did this by indexing using logical vectors
```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
flights[flights$month == 1 & 
          flights$day == 1, ]
```


## Filtering on Multiple Values

Just like we saw before when learning about logical vectors, there's multiple ways to do this.

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
filter(flights, month == 11 | month == 12)
filter(flights, month %in% c(11, 12))
```

## Missing Value Handling

Missing values (```NA```) are handled in natural ways by ```filter```
```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
filter(flights, 
       !(arr_delay > 120 | 
           dep_delay > 120))
```

Before, we would have needed to type
```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
flights[!is.na(flights$arr_delay) & 
          !is.na(flights$dep_delay) & 
          flights$arr_delay <= 120 & 
          flights$dep_delay <= 120, ]
```

## Filtering Using Intervals

The ```between``` function with ```left``` and ```right``` arguments allow us to filter on variables being in an interval.
```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
filter(flights, arr_delay <= 120, 
       between(x = dep_delay, left = 80, right = 120))
```

This is much uglier with base ```R```!
```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
flights[!is.na(flights$arr_delay) & 
          !is.na(flights$dep_delay) & 
          flights$arr_delay <= 120 & 
          flights$dep_delay >= 80 & 
          flights$dep_delay <= 120, ]
```

## Letting Missing Values Through

Sometimes, we want to retain some observations with missing values.
```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
filter(flights, is.na(arr_delay) | 
         arr_delay <= 120, 
       between(x = dep_delay, left = 80, right = 120))
```

In base ```R``` this would have been
```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
flights[!is.na(flights$dep_delay) & 
          flights$arr_delay <= 120 & 
          flights$dep_delay >= 80 & 
          flights$dep_delay <= 120, ]
```

## Activities to Try Yourself

Find all flights that were:

- Delayed two or more hours
- Flew to Houston 
- Were operated by United, American, or Delta
- Departed in summer (July, August, and September)
- Arrived more than two hours late, but didn’t leave late
- Delayed at least an hour, but made up over 30 minutes in flight

## The ```arrange``` Function

The ```arrange``` function allows us to sort data frames easily by multiple variables

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
arrange(flights, year, month, day)
```

Again, we could have done this in base ```R```
```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
flights[order(flights$year, flights$month, flights$day), ]
```

## Sorting in Reverse

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
arrange(flights, desc(dep_delay))
```

Note: This is starting to look like SQL!

## The ```select``` Function

The ```select``` function allows us to subset variables

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
select(flights, year, month, day)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
select(flights, year:day)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
select(flights, -(year:day))
```

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
select(flights, time_hour, air_time, everything())
```

## The ```rename``` Function

The ```rename``` function lets us subset multiple variables at once.

```{r, eval = FALSE,  echo = TRUE}
renamed <- rename(flights, tail_num = tailnum)
```

This would have been much more code in base ```R```!

```{r, eval = FALSE,  echo = TRUE}
renamed <- flights
renamed$tail_num <- flights$tailnum
renamed$tailnum <- NULL
```

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
renamed <- flights
names(renamed)[names(renamed) == "tailnum"] <- 
  "tail_num"
```

## The ```mutate``` Function

The ```mutate``` function makes it easy to construct new variables.

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
flightsnew <- mutate(flights,
                     gain = dep_delay - arr_delay,
                     speed = distance / air_time * 60)
```

This would also be a pain in base ```R```
```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
flightsnew <- flights
flightsnew$gain <- flightsnew$dep_delay - 
  flightsnew$arr_delay
flightsnew$speed <- flightsnew$distance/
  flightsnew$air_time * 60
```

## The ```mutate``` Function

The ```mutate``` function even allows you to use newly defined variables to define other new variables

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
flightsnew2 <- mutate(flights,
                      gain = dep_delay - arr_delay,
                      hours = air_time / 60,
                      gain_per_hour = gain / hours)
```

This would **really** be a pain in base ```R```
```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
flightsnew2 <- flights
flightsnew2$gain <- flightsnew2$dep_delay - flightsnew2$arr_delay
flightsnew2$hours <- flightsnew2$air_time/60
flightsnew2$gain_per_hour <-  flightsnew2$gain/flightsnew2$hours
```

## The ```transmute``` Function

The ```transmute``` function is similar to ```mutate```, but drops variables that aren't modified

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
flightsnew2 <- transmute(flights,
                         gain = dep_delay - arr_delay,
                         hours = air_time / 60,
                         gain_per_hour = gain / hours)
head(flightsnew2)
```

## The ```summarize``` Function

The ```summarize``` function allows us to create aggregate summaries

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
summarise(flights, delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))
```

This was easy to do  in base ```R```
```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
mean(flights$dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## Aggregating within Groups

When combined with ```group_by```, we can also construct aggregate summaries within levels of other variables

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
bymy <- summarise(group_by(flights, year, month), 
                  delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Doing this in base ```R``` requires the aggregate function
```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
bymy <- aggregate(flights$dep_delay, 
                  list("year" = flights$year, 
                       "month" = flights$month), 
                  mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## Aggregating within Groups - Comparison

\footnotesize

The output of ```summarize``` is much nicer

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
summarise(group_by(flights, year, month), 
          delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))[1, ]
```

Doing this in base ```R``` requires the aggregate function
```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
aggregate(flights$dep_delay, 
          list("year" = flights$year, 
               "month" = flights$month), 
          mean, na.rm = TRUE)[1, ]
```

## Creating Multiple Aggregate Variables

This becomes **much** easier with ```dplyr``` than base `R`
```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
bymy <- summarise(group_by(flights, year, month), 
                  delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
                  dist = mean(distance, na.rm = TRUE),
                  count = n())
```

## Creating Multiple Aggregate Variables (Base)

\footnotesize
In base ```R```, we need to create the new variables one at a time and then merge them together. Ugh!
```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
dep_delaymeans <- aggregate(flights$dep_delay, 
                       list("year" = flights$year, 
                            "month" = flights$month), 
                       mean, na.rm = TRUE)
colnames(dep_delaymeans)[ncol(dep_delaymeans)] <- "dep_delay"
distmeans <- aggregate(flights$dist, 
                            list("year" = flights$year, 
                                 "month" = flights$month), 
                            mean, na.rm = TRUE)
colnames(distmeans)[ncol(distmeans)] <- "dist"
distcounts <- aggregate(flights$dist, 
                            list("year" = flights$year, 
                                 "month" = flights$month), 
                            length)
colnames(distcounts)[ncol(distcounts)] <- "n"
bymy <- merge(distmeans, dep_delaymeans, by = c("month", "year"))
bymy <- merge(bymy, distcounts, by = c("month", "year"))
```

## A Diversion on Merging

We learned about merging (joining) in SQL. What about ```R```?

We use the ```merge``` function.
```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
bymy <- merge(bymy, distcounts, by = c("month", "year"),
              all.x = TRUE, all.y = TRUE)
```

The arguments ```all.x``` and ```all.y``` refer to the first and second data frames provided and determine if it is a left, right, or inner join.

## Creating Aggregate Variables without Aggregating Data

Combining ```mutate``` with ```group_by``` lets us add summaries to the original data
```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
mutate(group_by(flights, year, month), 
       dep_delay_bymonth = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))
```

In base ```R```, this always involves multiple steps
```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
delaypermonth <- aggregate(flights$dep_delay, 
                           list("month" = flights$month), 
                       mean, na.rm = TRUE)
names(delaypermonth)[ncol(delaypermonth)] <- 
  "dep_delay_bymonth"
flightsnew5 <- merge(flights, delaypermonth, by = "month")
```

## Grouping the Data

Sometimes, it can be beneficial to group the data as a separate command before applying ``summarize``` or ```mutate```

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
flights <- group_by(flights, dest)
delay <- summarise(flights,
                   count = n(),
                   dist = mean(distance, na.rm = TRUE),
                   delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE))
delay <- filter(delay, count > 20, dest != "HNL")
```

Note: Ungroup after with ```flights <- ungroup(flights)```!! Otherwise any use of ```summarize```, ```mutate```, or ```transmute``` after will use the grouping you previously provided.

## Aggregating at Different Levels

For a single analysis, we may want to aggregate at multiple levels

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
flights <- group_by(flights, dest)
delay <- summarise(flights,
                   count = n(),
                   dist = mean(distance, na.rm = TRUE),
                   delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE))
delay <- filter(delay, count > 20, dest != "HNL")
```


## The Pipe Operator

A big selling point of using ```dplyr``` is the incorporation of the pipe operator ```|>```

- Originated from an external package, was ```%>%```
- ```|>``` is the base ```R``` equivalent of ```%>%```, is now preferred over ```%>%```

## Use of ```|>```

The pipe operator  ```|>``` passes output from one function to another function as the first argument. 

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
delay <- flights |> 
  group_by(dest) |>
  summarize(count = n(),
                   dist = mean(distance, na.rm = TRUE),
                   delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  filter(count > 20, dest != "HNL")
```

## To Summarize

We have learned about:

- ```filter```
- ```arrange```
- ```select```
- ```rename```
- ```mutate```
- ```transmute```
